idiom_name: java.lang.ref.WeakReference on the JVM; kotlin.native.ref.WeakReference on Kotlin/Native (expect/actual)
implementation_notes: Kotlin has no weak-reference type of its own on the JVM: the realization is java.lang.ref.WeakReference together with the JDK's WeakHashMap and ReferenceQueue, and Kotlin's null safety only changes the call site - get() still returns a nullable T, and the promotion must be checked and held in a local. Kotlin/Native ships kotlin.native.ref.WeakReference with the same shape (get(): T? and clear()), so a multiplatform codebase declares an expect/actual weak-reference abstraction and binds it to the platform class per target; Android code uses the JVM class in the conventional leak-prone spots (listener registries, handler maps, adapters holding a Context). No Kotlin idiom removes the promotion step, and no Kotlin collection is weak out of the box.
pitfalls: get() returns T? and can turn null between two reads: promote once into a local (val l = ref.get() ?: return) instead of calling get() repeatedly around other work.

A lambda that captures this keeps the enclosing object alive regardless of the reference type around it, so a listener stored as WeakReference still leaks if the listener lambda closes over the Activity.

Kotlin/Native's WeakReference is a different class from the JVM one, so an expect/actual declaration must not leak either platform type into a common API, and native GC behaviour differs from the JVM's.
